why: A frozen meal maker selling 2.5 million salmon bakes a year, each with 0.1 kg of salmon at $15 to $19 per kg and $1.20 of other inputs, is believable.
Gym chains of 40 and 90 sites using about 120 to 150 MWh per gym a year, with cost shares and margins that add to 100% for each chain, are believable.
A tax preparer whose returns and hours peak at the deadline, with seasonal hours always below total hours and permanent hours steady at 80 to 105, is believable.
A regional brewer selling $530m through 670 distributors, with sales shares that add to 100% and 39 to 58 days to pay, is believable.
A national grocery chain with $12.9bn of sales whose channel bars add exactly to the total, and online at about a fifth of sales, is believable.
A hotel trial with 17,000 reviews where every rating distribution adds to 100% is believable.
A trade magazine publisher with 12 titles earning $1m to $41m each, about $154m in total, and 202 journalists is believable even though it is loss-making.
Portable toilet rental at $60 a week, a truck costing $1,500 a day and about 50 services a day per truck are high or low but within a factor of a few of real figures.

The countries are said to be ordered biggest to smallest, but the cumulative series shows country 5 adding 5.5 points after country 4 added 4.4, country 7 adding 3.7 after country 6 added 2.7, and country 38 adding 1.1 after country 37 added nothing, so the figures contradict the stated order.
A package holiday firm with $290m booked through 1,210 agents, shares adding to 100% and cancellation rates of 9% to 14%, is believable.
